title: Making a Shared Workspace Work
instructions: Listen carefully. Choose the option that best matches what is said or implied.

audio.description: Colleagues discuss feedback and changes to a shared office arrangement.

transcript.text: The shared workspace has been open six weeks. People like choosing where to sit, but the quiet area is not staying quiet; teams hold discussions there.
They are not trying to disturb anyone. Often they cannot find an empty meeting room. We should clarify each area’s purpose before introducing stricter rules.
We could mark one side for quiet work. I would not ban brief conversations entirely, since people sometimes need to ask a quick question without booking a room.
We should check the booking system too. Yesterday it showed two rooms free, but both were in use.
People may forget to cancel. A reminder after half an hour could help, and teams could release rooms when plans change. That may improve capacity before we add rooms.
Several people mentioned glare on the window desks in the afternoon. Moving monitors could help, but make the desks less flexible for laptop users.
Let’s test adjustable blinds first. Facilities can check the cost, and regular users can tell us whether it helps. A couple of comments are not enough reason to buy equipment.
We had over forty feedback replies, so we understand common concerns. Still, we do not know whether the same people replied or whether the layout works for everyone.
We can keep the layout another month and ask people who have not used the form. Include remote staff, who may have different needs on team days.
They may need a predictable desk when they arrive. We could let them reserve one, while keeping most desks free for unplanned visits.
Let’s update signs, fix calendar reminders, and test blinds. We can review results at month’s end before deciding on larger changes.
We should explain why each change is a trial. People may then feel more comfortable saying honestly what helps and what does not.

questions.prompt: What is one problem with the quiet area?
options: People are having discussions there.
The desks cannot be moved.
It is only open in the afternoon.
The area is difficult to find.
questions.explanation: The feedback shows the quiet area is not staying quiet because teams use it for discussions.

questions.prompt: Why does Colleague B hesitate to introduce stricter rules immediately?
options: The workspace is closing soon.
The signs are too expensive.
People may be talking because meeting rooms are unavailable.
Nobody has complained about noise.
questions.explanation: They observe that people often cannot find an empty meeting room and may be talking there for that reason.

questions.prompt: What might be causing the calendar to show rooms as free when they are occupied?
options: The rooms are being renovated.
People forget to cancel reservations.
The calendar only updates at night.
Remote staff are booking them twice.
questions.explanation: Colleague A suggests people may forget to cancel when plans change.

questions.prompt: Why do they want to test blinds before buying equipment?
options: They need to reduce the number of desks.
The monitors cannot be moved.
They have already spent the budget on signs.
They want evidence that the change solves the glare problem.
questions.explanation: They propose checking the cost and asking regular users whether blinds help rather than buying equipment based on a few comments.

questions.prompt: What does the final plan suggest about their approach?
options: They intend to remove all shared desks.
They will apply every suggestion immediately.
They prefer small trials and later review before making wider changes.
They believe the feedback form is unreliable and should be ignored.
questions.explanation: They agree to test signs, reminders, and blinds, then review the results at month end before deciding on bigger changes.
